10
11
12
13

tests/
├── api/
│ └── users.api.spec.ts
├── ui/
│ └── users.ui.spec.ts
├── webmcp/
│ ├── contract.spec.ts # exposed tools and schemas
│ ├── authorization.spec.ts # capabilities by role
│ ├── validation.spec.ts # input boundary attacks
│ ├── security.spec.ts # unexpected capabilities and dangerous metadata
│ └── integration.spec.ts # real backend side effects
└── fixtures/
 └── webmcp.fixture.ts

The five files each map to one class of risk, their responsibilities do not overlap, and attribution of failures is straightforward.

Three Principles Worth Remembering

First, the agent interface is a first-class contract; renaming, changing the schema or changing the description are all breaking changes and need tests to block them. Second, “not visible” does not equal “not executable”; authorization must be verified at the server boundary, and the tool discovery list is only a convenience at the UI level. Third, tool names, descriptions, schemas and returned results all come from the page and are untrusted input; once an LLM enters the architecture, this data influences the agent’s subsequent behaviour, so tests cannot stop at expect(result.isError).toBeFalsy().

The browser is changing from “an object driven by automation frameworks” into “a runtime where humans, applications and autonomous agents operate together”. Playwright already has DOM automation, API testing, network interception, WebSocket mocking, time control, accessibility snapshots and tracing, and now it has added inspection and execution of WebMCP tools. For testing teams this means a question that did not exist before has to be answered inside the regression suite: not “can a user successfully operate the application through the browser”, but “can an AI agent operate the application through the browser safely and correctly”. The answers to those two questions are not the same.

item.title: Why Mobile E2E Tests Go Flaky - Four Failure Modes Web Testing Never Meets
item.description:
Retries are not a fix. Longer timeouts are not a fix. A quarantine list is not a fix. And that shared Slack channel the team set up specifically for “known flaky, safe to ignore”, that is even less of a fix.

Most testing teams agree with these sentences, but the real issue is this: mobile E2E tests are unstable for reasons that are simply not of the same kind as those behind web tests; and every solution borrowed from the web playbook makes the problem structurally worse.

A recurring sequence looks like this: a team takes over an end-to-end suite, adds automatic retries when tests start failing, lengthens timeouts when retries are not enough, and finally stops trusting the cases altogether. Nobody looks when CI goes red, and nobody knows whether it is a real defect or “just another ordinary Tuesday”.

This is not a discipline problem. The problem is that mobile E2E has four failure modes that simply do not exist on the web, and web-first fixes drag the wrong mental model along with them.

Mobile Instability Is a Different Problem

Web automation runs inside a browser. The browser is a sandboxed, largely deterministic environment: the DOM is queryable, animations can be disabled, network requests can be intercepted, and the rendering engine behaves predictably across runs. When web tests go flaky, the causes are long since well studied – async waits, test order dependencies, shared state pollution; every testing textbook covers them.

Mobile automation runs on top of a whole operating system, and that difference invalidates every assumption inherited from web testing.

A mobile app test has to cope with system-level interruptions the test script never triggered; has to cope with a gesture model where “a 10 millisecond difference in click timing changes the result”; has to survive CI emulators that behave differently on the 47th run than on the first; and has to produce consistent results across a device ecosystem that, on Android alone, spans thousands of vendors and dozens of still-active OS versions.

Fixing mobile flakiness with web solutions is like diagnosing an aircraft hydraulic fault with an automobile brake repair manual: the vocabulary overlaps, the physics do not.

Those web-oriented fixes (unified async waiting patterns, isolated test state, enforced test order) are correct for web problems. Applied to mobile, they probably solve half the problem; the other half has different causes and needs different solutions.

The data shows this has not improved as tooling matured. An industry report on mobile development covering three years and more than ten million builds showed that the share of mobile teams reporting flaky tests rose from 10% in 2022 to 26% in 2025. The more complex the pipeline, the worse the instability.

Top: emulator responsiveness keeps degrading as a run progresses; bottom: the decision boundaries of gesture timing are not evenly spaced

Four Failure Modes Web Testing Has Never Seen

One: Emulator Behaviour Drift

CI pipelines run on emulators, not real devices. An emulator is a software simulation of hardware, and like any software running in a resource-constrained CI environment, its behaviour degrades continuously over the course of a single test run.

At the start of a suite the emulator responds well: GPU acceleration is warm, memory is clean, the virtual CPU has headroom. Forty cases later the same emulator may be under memory pressure, the virtual CPU may be throttling, or it may start dropping gesture events because the event queue is backed up. The test code is identical; the environment has drifted.

Web CI environments do not have a problem of the same scale, because browser instances are lightweight and stateless. An emulator runs an entire mobile operating system: camera drivers, Bluetooth stack, network simulation, GPS simulation – all of it runs even if your test only touches one login page.

The typical symptom: cases at positions 1-15 pass reliably, and by positions 30-50 they start failing intermittently. The developer’s reaction is to add retries; retries occasionally work because the second attempt happens to catch a moment when the emulator state is slightly better; and the root cause – the emulator changed behaviour mid-run – is never addressed.

Two: Gesture Timing Sensitivity

The essence of mobile interaction is the gesture. A tap is not a click and a swipe is not a scroll, and that difference matters far more than it sounds.

A browser click triggers a discrete set of events (mousedown, mouseup, click) that the DOM handles predictably. A mobile gesture is a stream of touch events with time attributes, interpreted by the operating system in context: holding for 100 milliseconds is a tap, holding for 500 milliseconds triggers a long-press context menu; a swipe that starts 5 pixels further left may be recognised as a scroll rather than a swipe on a particular device or OS version.

Automation frameworks do expose gesture APIs, but the underlying timing behaviour differs between iOS and Android, between OS versions, and between emulators and real devices. A gesture command that is stable on a local emulator may fail on a CI host with different virtualisation characteristics. Long lists usually expose this difference first, because a fast swipe crosses a different number of rows each time – which is why infinite-scroll tests usually swipe one step at a time and then wait for the target cell to appear.

The web does not have this problem; click events are abstracted away at the browser layer. Mobile developers have no equivalent abstraction layer and must work directly against an OS gesture model that varies by implementation.

Three: System Permission Dialogs

iOS and Android pop system-level permission dialogs during app flows: camera, microphone, location, notifications, contacts, Bluetooth. These dialogs are not triggered by your test; the operating system decides when to show them based on internal state.

Once a dialog appears mid-test it covers the interface. The script tries to click an element that is now obscured, the click fails, the element is not found, and the test reports a failure that has nothing to do with the code under test.

When the dialog appears is not fully deterministic: a clean emulator state may not show the notification permission on the first run but may show it on the third, because by then the app has been installed long enough for the system to decide it is time to ask. Teams respond by adding “dismiss the dialog” logic to test setup; but system behaviour changes with iOS and Android versions, so a setup script that works on one version silently stops working on another.

This class of flakiness is especially expensive, because the failure report points at the wrong element – the one the script wanted to click, not the dialog that actually blocked it.

Four: Network Conditions and Device Fragmentation

Mobile apps run under network conditions web apps largely avoid: switching between WiFi and cellular, the app being backgrounded mid-request, carrier-specific DNS behaviour, and latency that varies with signal quality.

A test that passes on a WiFi-only emulator may fail on a real device when it switches to cellular mid-flow; a test that handles a 200 millisecond API response may fail in a CI environment whose network simulation is configured differently. These are not async waiting problems but environment fidelity problems: the test environment and real operating conditions do not match.

Device fragmentation amplifies it further. The Android ecosystem stretches from entry-level phones with 1GB of memory running Android 9 all the way to current flagship hardware. A test designed for “a high-spec virtual machine plus an Android 14 emulator” will meet differences in rendering timing, memory management and garbage collection behaviour on real entry-level hardware. Screen density differences alone are enough to make a click coordinate that works on one device miss on another.

Selector-based suites assume the view hierarchy is stable across devices – and it frequently is not.

Why Script-Level Fixes Make Things Worse

Facing mobile flakiness, the standard move is a predictable escalation path: retry first, because it is the least effortful lever; then add timeouts, because more time usually lets emulator drift and gesture timing eventually slip through; then quarantine, because some cases are reliably unreliable and the team simply stops expecting them to pass.

Each has a cost, and none of it shows up on the CI dashboard.

Retries mask real failures. A case that passes on the third retry is a flaky case that got lucky; it may equally be a real regression buried by the retry logic. One widely cited study found that flakiness caused 84% of “pass to fail” state transitions in its test suites – meaning teams that rely on retries are habitually attributing real regressions to “just flakiness”. The confidence signal the suite is supposed to provide is no longer trustworthy.

Longer timeouts slow the suite without touching the root cause. Extending a gesture timeout from 3 seconds to 8 seconds does cover “the emulator needs more time to process gesture events”, but it also adds 5 seconds to every run of that case. A suite of 200 cases with 3 extra seconds of timeout buffer each runs 10 minutes longer overall. A longer feedback loop means developers have already switched to the next task by the time they learn about a failure.

Quarantine postpones the problem to a future that never arrives. “We will fix the quarantined cases next iteration” almost never happens, because fixing them requires understanding the root cause, and understanding the root cause requires environmental investigation that is slower than writing new cases. So the quarantine list grows longer; and the quarantined cases represent real coverage holes – regressions hide in those holes.

The common problem with all three is the same: treating a structural problem as a maintenance problem. Flakiness is not because the team is not careful enough, but because selector-based tests couple cases to UI implementation details, and those details keep changing as the app evolves, the OS updates and the CI environment drifts.

Public data from one engineering team shows that even with heavy investment in detection and monitoring tooling, 15-21% of builds were still affected by flakiness. Detection and monitoring can tell you which cases are broken, but they will not tell you why mobile-specific failure modes keep manufacturing new broken cases.

At some tipping point the ratio flips: a quality team starts out spending 90% of its time writing cases and 10% maintaining them; after the debt accumulates it becomes 10% writing and 90% maintaining. That compression is what the script-level fix treadmill looks like at team scale.

Five Practical Actions That Need No Tooling

Before discussing architecture-level solutions, there are things any team can do immediately that significantly reduce the four failure classes above:

  • Run each case on a clean emulator snapshot, or at least rebuild the emulator per batch, directly eliminating the root cause of “drift during a run”;
  • Preset permission state during test preparation (through launch arguments or system image configuration), rather than dismissing dialogs with scripts inside the flow;
  • Wrap gestures in an abstraction layer that always performs the interaction after real rendering state, instead of hard-coded wait constants scattered everywhere;
  • Adopt “single-step swipe plus wait for target to appear” for long lists and infinite scroll, instead of swipes that depend on inertia distance;
  • Tier the device matrix: run 2-3 representative configurations in the daily pipeline, and put fragmentation verification into separate, less frequent but broader batches.

These actions bring the total volume of flakiness down, but they cannot change one fact: as long as cases depend on selectors, UI changes, OS updates and device differences will keep manufacturing new failures.

The Architecture-Level Step: Removing the Selector Dependency

The selector-based model – locating elements by CSS selector, XPath, accessibility ID or resource ID – is precisely where the fragility of mobile cases comes from. Change an attribute and the case breaks; the system changes how the view hierarchy is structured and the case breaks; a layout adjustment moves an element 10 pixels and changes its bounds, and a case based on click coordinates breaks.

The alternative is to identify an element by what it looks like and what it does, rather than by implementation attributes. A “Submit” button is recognisable because it says “Submit”, appears in a particular position in the form, and responds to clicks. When that button is redesigned, moved, or given a different accessibility ID, visual identification can still recognise it the way a human tester would.

Looking back at the four failure modes from this angle, their roots all sit in the selector model:

  • Emulator drift causes gesture events to land on the wrong element, because element positions shift in a degraded emulator state – identifying by appearance does not depend on coordinates;
  • Gesture timing problems are amplified by hard-coded time constants – observe the actual rendering state before interacting and the timing assumption disappears;
  • System permission dialogs interrupt selector-based flows because the script is following an element path that is now obscured – identify by visual object and dismiss the dialog without changing the script for every OS version’s dialog format;
  • Device fragmentation breaks selector-based cases because layouts render differently across devices – identifying by “what the user sees” adapts to layout differences automatically.

It should be clear that this is not a feature you can install on top of an existing Appium or Detox suite, but a different test execution architecture: the user flows the cases verify stay the same, but they no longer depend on the implementation details that made those flows hard to maintain.

When evaluating this shift, the right question is not “can it eliminate all flakiness” – the answer is no, network faults and genuine environmental problems will still produce failures. The real question is whether flakiness caused by UI changes, device fragmentation and selector fragility (which is the majority of mobile-specific flakiness) becomes something you fix once at the architecture level, or remains a maintenance tax you pay every iteration.

Closing Thoughts

The loop is predictable: flakiness appears → add automatic retries → timeouts grow → the suite slows down → trust erodes → the team stops treating red CI as a signal worth investigating. This is not a discipline failure but the inevitable result of applying web testing assumptions to mobile testing problems.

The reasons mobile E2E fails simply do not exist in web automation. Emulator drift, gesture timing, system dialogs and device fragmentation are all mobile-specific problems that need mobile-specific structural solutions, not more layers of script-level patches.

And the maintenance treadmill has no sustainable pace. It has only one exit.

item.title: Using the Browser Console for Accessibility Testing - A Practical Script Collection
item.description:
At work, a few lines of JavaScript are all we need to highlight headings on any web page, check image alternative text, or inspect the distribution of landmarks.

The browser console is not just a developer debugging tool; it is also a sharp instrument for accessibility testing. By running simple scripts we can see the structure and accessibility features of a page directly, without changing the source code or installing complicated plugins.

What Is the Console?

The console is a tool built into modern browsers. It can:

  • Run temporary JavaScript code.

  • Quickly inspect page information.

  • Test ideas without changing the source code.

Code run in the console is valid only for the current session; refreshing the page restores everything.

How to Open the Console

  • On macOS:

    • Chrome: Option + Command + J

    • Firefox: Option + Command + K

    • Safari: first enable “Show Develop menu in menu bar” under “Settings → Advanced”, then press Option + Command + C.

  • On Windows:

    • Chrome / Edge / Firefox: Ctrl + Shift + J (or K)

Quick Start Examples

Before diving into complex scripts, try these two simple commands:

1. List all links on the page:

1

document.querySelectorAll("a");

2. Highlight all links on the page:

document.querySelectorAll("a").forEach(a => a.style.outline = "2px solid red");

14 Advanced Accessibility Testing Scripts

All the scripts below follow the same logic: create a transparent overlay at the top of the page, then add an outline and a floating badge to the corresponding elements.

item.title: A Closer Look at "Self-Healing" Technology in Test Automation
item.description:
If you have followed some of this year’s testing industry trend forecast articles, you will notice a frequently mentioned concept, Self-healing Test Automation, the self-healing technology for test scripts. So why is this technology a future trend, and what exactly is it?

In this article we will discuss this self-healing technology in test automation.

The Requirement Background That Produced This Technology

Traditional UI-based test automation has fairly strict requirements on the stability of the application under test. But with the wide adoption of agile development and DevOps, feature iteration and UI adjustments have become extremely frequent. To optimize performance or improve user experience, front-end development may often adjust the UI, such as changing a button’s ID, adjusting an input box’s CSS class name, or even refactoring the entire page’s DOM structure. These changes, trivial to developers, are fatal to traditional automation scripts that rely on precise element locators.

As a result, the testing team spends a lot of time every day maintaining these “fragile” scripts, frequently fixing failed cases caused by UI changes.

This high maintenance cost not only consumes precious human resources, but also destabilizes the CI/CD pipeline and slows down the entire delivery rhythm. Test automation is no longer an efficiency booster, but often becomes a “white elephant”.

Therefore, the market urgently needs a solution that reduces maintenance cost and improves script stability. It is against this background that self-healing technology emerged.

What Is Self-Healing

So what exactly is “self-healing”? It is no black magic, but an intelligent error recovery mechanism.

In short, self-healing test automation refers to the ability of a test script, during execution, when element location fails due to application UI changes, to automatically detect, analyze, and attempt to fix the problem so as to continue execution.

This process usually follows a closed loop of “detect - analyze - fix - verify”:

  1. Detect: When the test script throws an exception because it cannot find an element, the self-healing mechanism is triggered.
  2. Analyze: The system captures the current page’s DOM structure and compares it with the original element features recorded in the script (such as tag type, text content, CSS style, relative position, etc.) from multiple dimensions.
  3. Fix: Based on the analysis result, the system finds one or more most similar “candidate” elements on the current page and intelligently generates a new locating strategy (for example, switching from ID locating to XPath or text locating).
  4. Verify: The system retries the operation with the new locating strategy. If successful, it records this fix and continues with subsequent steps; if it fails, it marks the problem and reports it to the test engineer for manual intervention.

Script Self-Healing Is an Important Trend in Testing

As for why script self-healing technology is regarded as an important future trend, it is because it perfectly fits the core demands of modern software engineering.

First, it solves the core pain point of the DevOps era. In continuous integration and continuous delivery pipelines, stability and speed are lifelines. Self-healing technology, by greatly reducing invalid builds and test failures caused by UI changes, keeps the pipeline flowing and truly achieves “fast feedback”.

Second, it greatly improves the return on investment (ROI) of test automation. In the past, high maintenance costs deterred many enterprises from automation. Self-healing technology frees test engineers from tedious script repair work, allowing them to invest more energy in test case design, business logic verification, and other higher-value work, thus maximizing the value of automation.

Finally, it drives the transformation and upgrading of the test engineer role. Future testing experts are no longer simple “script writers”, but “quality architects” who know how to use AI and other intelligent tools to build more robust and efficient testing systems. Mastering and applying self-healing technology is a key step for testers to keep up with the technological wave and enhance their core competitiveness.

How Self-Healing Is Implemented

The implementation principles of self-healing technology can be divided into several levels, evolving from simple to complex:

  1. Rule-based and heuristic methods: This is the most basic implementation. The system has a series of built-in “if…then…” rules. For example, “if an element cannot be found by ID, look for a button with the same text content”, “if the XPath fails, look for an element with the same CSS class”. This method is simple and direct, but covers limited scenarios and lacks flexibility.

  2. Fuzzy matching of multiple element attributes: More advanced self-healing engines create a “feature fingerprint” for each element, containing its tag name, text, size, relative position on the page, and other attributes. When the original locator fails, the engine computes the “fingerprint” of all elements on the current page and finds the one with the highest similarity to the original “fingerprint” as the substitute target.

  3. Based on AI and machine learning: This is currently the most cutting-edge direction. By training machine learning models, the system learns from a large amount of page snapshots and locator data from successes and failures. The model can understand deeper page structures and element relationships, and even when the page changes significantly, it can accurately predict the correct target element, and even has some visual recognition capability, locating elements through image comparison.

A Technical Implementation Example

To help you understand this process more intuitively, we can use Python and Selenium to simulate a basic self-healing logic. This example combines the simple ideas of “rule-based” and “multi-attribute matching”.

Suppose our original locator is ID="submit-btn", but it has now failed. We also know the button’s text is “Submit Now”.

from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
from selenium.common.exceptions import NoSuchElementException

# --- core logic of a simulated self-healing engine ---
def smart_find_element(driver, original_locator, fallback_strategies):
 """
 A simplified self-healing find function that tries multiple locating strategies in order.

 :param driver: WebDriver instance
 :param original_locator: The original locator, as a tuple, e.g. (By.ID, "submit-btn")
 :param fallback_strategies: List of fallback strategies, each also a tuple
 :return: The found WebElement object
 """
 # Step 1: Try the original locator (normal flow)
 try:
 print(f"[Try] Using original locator: {original_locator}")
 element = driver.find_element(*original_locator)
 print("[Success] Element found!")
 return element
 except NoSuchElementException:
 # Steps 2 & 3: Failure detected, start analysis and fix (try fallback strategies)
 print(f"[Fail] Original locator invalid. Starting self-healing analysis, trying fallback strategies...")

 # Iterate over all fallback strategies
 for strategy in fallback_strategies:
 try:
 print(f"[Try] Using fallback strategy: {strategy}")
 healed_element = driver.find_element(*strategy)
 print(f"[Healed!] Matching element found, new locator: {strategy}")
 # In a real system, this successful fix would be recorded here for "learning"
 return healed_element
 except NoSuchElementException:
 print(f"[Strategy failed] Strategy {strategy} also did not find the element, trying the next one...")
 continue

 # All strategies failed
 print("[Self-healing failed] All fallback strategies exhausted, manual intervention needed.")
 raise NoSuchElementException("All locating strategies failed, unable to find the element.")

# --- test scenario ---

 # Original locator (By.ID, "submit-btn")

 # Define a set of fallback strategies, embodying the idea of "multi-attribute matching"
 fallback_strategies = [
 (By.PARTIAL_LINK_TEXT, "Submit Now"), # Strategy 1: match by partial text
 (By.CLASS_NAME, "primary-btn"), # Strategy 2: match by CSS class name
 (By.XPATH, "//button[contains(text(), 'Submit Now')]") # Strategy 3: match by more powerful XPath
 ]

 try:
 # In a real scenario, this would open the page and perform the lookup
 # submit_button = smart_find_element(driver, original_locator, fallback_strategies)
 # submit_button.click()
 print("Thought experiment: if run, smart_find_element will try the locators in order until it succeeds or all fail.")
 except Exception as e:
 print(f"Final operation failed: {e}")
 finally:
 driver.quit()

Through this simplified Python script, we demonstrated the flow of “detect - analyze - fix”. The smart_find_element function is our miniature self-healing engine. It first tries the original locator (detect); after failure, it tries new locating methods one by one according to our preset fallback strategy list (analyze, then fix).

Of course, a truly commercial-grade self-healing engine has “analysis” and “fix” algorithms far more complex than this; it dynamically generates locators rather than relying on a fixed fallback list, and makes comprehensive judgments based on dozens of dimensions such as DOM tree structure and element relative positions.

Further evolution can also build on AI technology to empower more intelligently and complete the transition from preset to prediction.

Advantages and Limitations

Every technology has two sides, and self-healing technology is no exception.

Advantages:

  • Significantly reduces maintenance cost: This is its core value.
  • Improves testing stability: Reduces “false positive” failures caused by environment changes.
  • Accelerates the release cycle: Keeps the CI/CD process smooth.
  • Improves team efficiency: Lets testers focus on more important tasks.

Limitations:

  • Not a panacea: For complex business logic changes or process refactoring, self-healing technology cannot help.
  • Risk of false positives: In some cases, the system may “self-heal” to the wrong element, masking a real functional defect.
  • Initial investment cost: Mature commercial self-healing tools are expensive, while in-house development requires a high technical threshold.
  • Needs manual supervision: The fixes proposed by the self-healing system still need review and confirmation by test engineers to ensure accuracy.

Conclusion

In summary, self-healing test automation cannot replace the work of test engineers, but provides them with a powerful “intelligent assistant”. Through intelligent means, it effectively solves the thorny maintenance problems in traditional test automation, giving it greater adaptability in a fast-iterating development environment.

Through the implementation of self-healing technology, the testing team can build a more resilient, more efficient quality assurance system with higher ROI. It is a development direction that testing teams can focus on investing in going forward.

In previous articles, we introduced various browser AI automation tools such as Playwright-mcp, browser-use, and midsceneJs; each can well drive a browser to complete automated tasks based on AI large models.

Recently, Google officially launched the devtools mcp for the Chrome browser, further enriching the tools for driving a browser to complete intelligent tasks through AI, including executing automated test scripts.

What Is DevTools MCP?

In short, DevTools MCP is Google exposing the underlying devtools methods of the Chrome browser, based on the MCP (Model Context Protocol) standard, to AI large language models (LLMs) as a service, enabling AI large models to call the underlying debugging tools of the Chrome browser.

For a detailed introduction to MCP, see my previous article 【】

Chrome DevTools MCP Architecture

The tool uses a layered architecture, mainly including the following modules:

  • MCP Server layer: Responsible for receiving MCP requests from the LLM/agent, and performing session management and permission control.
  • Tool adaptation layer: Maps MCP’s high-level requests to the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) or Puppeteer API, and manages long tasks (such as recording/tracing).
  • Chrome runtime: A real Chrome/Chromium instance (headful or headless) that performs all underlying operations and produces trace, performance, console, and other data.
  • Data collection and transmission: Serializes the collected trace, stack, HAR, snapshots, and other data, and returns it to the caller via MCP.

The specific calling process is shown below:

Tool Methods Exposed by Chrome DevTools MCP

Debugging 4 evaluate_script, list_console_messages, take_screenshot, take_snapshot

Emulation 3 emulate_cpu, emulate_network, resize_page

- Introduce a performance budget, set thresholds for image size, CSS/JS size, and request count, and check automatically in CI.

When selecting AI automation tools, it is worth considering as a preferred direction.

item.title: Test Automation - Pre-made Meals vs. Chef Made to Order
item.description:
Recently, Xibei and Luo Yonghao set off a heated debate online over pre-made meals, which clearly touched a nerve among netizens.

I do not want to discuss the rights and wrongs of pre-made meals here, but thinking about the quality field, test automation and manual testing seem just like the difference between pre-made meals and chef made to order. This article expands on this thought experiment.

Test Automation and the “Pre-made Meal” Logic

In modern software development, test automation is undoubtedly a powerful tool for improving efficiency and safeguarding basic quality. Like pre-made meals, it has the huge advantage of being standardized and reproducible, helping teams deliver quickly in fast-paced iterations. But it also shares the obvious drawbacks of pre-made meals.

The Advantages of “Pre-made Meals”

Just as efficiency is the main advantage of “pre-made meals”, once automation scripts are written, they can run repeatedly without limit, efficiently avoiding human omissions and execution-efficiency problems in regression testing. They effectively solve the efficiency bottleneck of large-scale, repetitive verification.

The Limitations of Pre-made Meals

  • Loss of freshness: Just as what people criticize most about pre-made meals is the freshness of the dishes, automation scripts likewise can only target stable business scenarios and flows (ingredients); once the product changes, automation scripts easily become invalid.

  • Additives: To keep the taste of the dishes, pre-made meals often use various additives or heavy seasoning. Similarly, in automation scripts, to ensure the flow runs smoothly, mocks or workarounds are often needed to bypass certain user scenarios (such as CAPTCHAs).

  • The missing wok hei: Pre-made meals rarely have the wok hei of freshly cooked dishes, and automation scripts always verify only known expected results. They are poor at capturing subtle changes in business logic and the humanized design of new features, and even less able to empathize with user experience (UX).

Pre-made meals use a pre-fixed production process, so a dish can be made with minimal effort; test automation uses pre-written test scripts, so test results can be obtained quickly by triggering execution.

But because of the limits of ingredients and production techniques, pre-made meals necessarily cover only a limited range of products and can only meet basic requirements, so they are hard to equate with high-quality products.

Manual Testing - Testing a Product Is Like Cooking a Small Fish

Just as real deliciousness cannot do without the smoke and fire of cooking, manual testing is the “chef made to order” in quality assurance.

Exploratory Testing

What is “wok hei”? It is the deliciousness achieved by the chef adapting to the ingredients amid the shifting smoke and fire.

Testing is the same; many product quality problems only emerge during deep exploration in the testing process.

Experienced test engineers, like chefs, rely more on rich experience and intuition, and during product testing (cooking) discover the traces of product quality problems according to differences in color, aroma, taste, and heat.

In real user scenarios, the user experience is also beyond the reach of test automation: whether a button on a mobile app is easy to tap, whether the swiping feels smooth - these are hard to measure quantitatively with automation scripts.

Automation can only judge whether an element “exists”, not whether it is “usable”.

Complementing Each Other

Pre-made meals are actually an inevitable trend for the catering industry in the context of scale and industrialization, but they will certainly not be the only choice; in the current era they can only serve as a low-end supplement.

And test automation and manual testing, as quality assurance means, are just like the difference between pre-made and made to order.

We can hand repetitive, standardized module verification to automation scripts, and leave deep exploration, complex logic, and verification requiring subjective creativity to the “chefs”!

item.title: Is Shift-Left Testing Ineffective in Agile?
item.description:
Saw a question on a Q&A site about shift-left testing not delivering results; here I share Qiucao’s answer

Summary

The questioner’s problem is actually not simply a matter of how to shift testing left. The so-called “testing becoming a bottleneck” is more the result of various problems piling up.

And applying agile development does not mean it is agile just because you run an iteration every two weeks. From the question, we can see that this iteration actually still ran as a mini-waterfall, still with requirements, design, test submission, testing; the team did not actually become agile.

Challenge Analysis

Let’s first analyze the many challenges the questioner mentioned:

  1. Incomplete requirements documents

Agile indeed does not emphasize documentation, but that does not mean requirements within an iteration can be unclear and incomplete.

In agile practice, before an iteration begins, the PO should have completed the PBI list and worked with the team to complete requirements grooming. And an important condition for starting an iteration is that at the sprint planning meeting, the team jointly confirms the SBI and the workload. Uncertain requirements should not enter the SBI.

Of course, agile embraces change; changes and additions to requirements during an iteration are possible, but it is not advocated to have them frequently within an iteration, because with fixed team productivity, changes cause WIP artifacts to change, and burndown charts and velocity charts will deviate from the ideal curve. Mature agile teams avoid such situations as much as possible.

  1. Low developer involvement in testing

An agile team actually does not define two different roles, development and testing. That is, in agile, there is no absolute division of labor between development and testing.

“Eating your own dog food” is a phrase often mentioned in agile practice, which essentially makes clear the necessity of developer self-testing.

Agile in which developers do not test is necessarily pseudo-agile.

  1. The team lacks an effective communication mechanism

This is even harder to explain.

All agile principles and practices are fundamentally aimed at breaking down barriers and improving communication and collaboration efficiency. If it is still hard for the team, especially development and testing, to communicate, then this is simply not agile at all.

So, first make agile actually agile, then look at the results of shift-left testing.

Should We Implement Shift-Left Testing?

What does the questioner’s shift-left look like?

Have testers get involved in requirements review earlier, and also try to write more detailed test plans, but the effect is not obvious

  • First, we need to stress again that in an agile team there is no separate role of tester; apart from PO and SM, all members are the Dev Team. So there is no such thing as “letting testers participate in requirements review earlier” - in requirements grooming and SBI determination, testing should necessarily be involved.

  • As for more detailed test plans, this is actually weakened in agile; agile advocates test strategies like one-page plans, where clarifying 6W2H before testing is enough.

So the so-called shift-left here is originally the normal operation of testing.

Even in waterfall mode, requirements review and test planning are things testers should participate in.

This is not real shift-left!

How to Shift Left

So in agile, when we talk about shift-left testing, what should actually be done?

The normal understanding is still early participation in requirements review and design review, as well as pairing with developers while coding, assisting with unit testing, and so on.

But I want to say that real shift-left testing in agile is not simply moving testing activities left. Testing activities should run through the entire development activity, and every team member should carry them out and be responsible for them.

Just as BDD and ATDD practices follow the adoption of agile, the starting point of shift-left should be concrete business and user acceptance scenarios. Or more directly, the requirements themselves.

Shift-left testing should be more about testers, as a quality perspective within the team, injecting quality and risk control genes from the very beginning (from when the PO creates requirements), and helping the whole team build and popularize quality awareness and conduct risk control.

Improving quality and efficiency by a single testing role alone is empty talk. Only when the whole team values quality and embeds risk avoidance into all activities from the very beginning is it fundamental.

item.title: A Fun Bug Story - The Norway Problem
item.description:
In the previous series, we shared the origin of Bug, some close relatives similar to Bug, and also an interesting classic Bug. In this article we share another very typical Bug, one that the author has personally encountered.

A Strange Page Crash

The author once tested a web application related to import and export trade. One page displayed information about trading partners, similar to the figure below.

There was an auxiliary feature that could export transaction information as a standard-format document meeting the requirements of the counterparty’s country (of course, the format is actually the same for most countries).

This feature showed no problems during testing.

But after delivery to users, at one particular customer, once this export operation was triggered, the page would intermittently crash - a serious problem.

Locating the Problem

After receiving this feedback several times, it was found that whenever this user experienced the crash, without exception, the counterparty’s trading country was Norway, and the document exported for that country was also a standard document. So it was not a problem with the exported document format.

After analyzing the implementation logic of this feature, the crux of the problem was finally found.

In this export feature, the matching of document formats is defined in a YAML configuration file, and country identification is configured in YAML via country codes. And Norway’s country code is NO

Something like:

1
2
3
4

config:
 - filetype: pdf
 - profile: standard
 - country: NO

According to the definition in the YAML V1.1 standard specification (https://yaml.org/type/bool.html):

After the code interprets NO, it is treated as the boolean value False. And the program here lacks configuration validation and exception protection, causing an exception when reading the country code and resulting in a page crash.

So the causes can be summarized as:

  1. YAML configuration file: the country code configuration is treated as a string by default, without considering special cases like NO, and no string quotes were added.
  2. Program handling: lacks validation of the correctness of YAML configuration values.
  3. Insufficient exception protection: an exception directly causes the page to crash.

Fixing the Problem

Once the cause is found, the fix is actually very simple: for the country code, force-convert it to a string before processing, and add validity checks and exception protection code. Of course, for YAML configurations that easily cause ambiguity, string quotes were also added.

1
2
3
4

config:
 - filetype: pdf
 - profile: standard
 - country: "NO"

Reflection

Actually it is not just country codes. In string-type fields, using other characters with special meanings, such as “Yes”, “null”, etc., can also cause similar problems.

Therefore, for us in testing, data handling verification during testing, especially the handling of similar special characters, must take relevant scenarios into account; otherwise it is easy to miss similar serious problems.

A Fun Bug Story - The 500-Mile Email

Let’s continue sharing classic Bugs from history.

This Bug is also quite bizarre:

The story takes place in 2002. That day, the head of the statistics department at MIT approached Trey Harris, the person in charge of the campus email system, complaining about a rather bizarre problem: “Our emails can’t reach anywhere beyond 500 miles. Actually, 520 miles is more accurate.” The admin’s inner voice: ^&^(&………&))(&^% But no matter how hard he disbelieved it, he still tested it himself with his own mailbox. The result was actually true! Just as reported, emails could only be sent within 520 miles, and any email beyond that range failed to send.

After some investigation, the cause was finally figured out.

It turned out that not long before, the operating system of the mail server had just been upgraded (still SunOS back then), and OS distributions at that time usually came bundled with some accessory software, but the versions of these pieces of software were often quite old (just like updating Linux, the bundled Python version is usually not the latest). So after the system update, the version of the mail software they used, SendMail, was downgraded (SendMail 8 -> SendMail 5).

And updating the system also kept SendMail’s configuration file sendmail.cfg, so the following situation arose: SendMail 5 would parse SendMail 8’s configuration file.

Because sendmail.cfg contained a configuration item timeout to connect to the remote SMTP server that SendMail 5 did not support, that is, the timeout for connecting to the remote SMTP server. For this unsupported configuration, SendMail 5 simply ignored it and treated it as the default value 0. And later experiments showed that a timeout of 0 seconds would cause Sendmail to interrupt the connection after 3 milliseconds.

So why 500 miles?

Back then, there were not many routers in MIT’s campus network, so network latency was very low - that is, the time to connect to a remote host was roughly close to the speed of light. So 3 milliseconds meant:

0.003 * 3 * 10 ^ 8 * 0.001 * 0.621 = 558.9

Considering the low network latency, this is how the 500-mile problem came about.

item.title: ISTQB CT-GenAI Expert Level Certification for Testing with Generative AI Explained
item.description:
Preface

The International Software Testing Qualifications Board (ISTQB®) officially released the Expert Level Certification Syllabus - Testing with Generative AI (CT-GenAI) v1.0 on July 25, 2025. This is the world’s first professional certification standard focused on the application of generative AI in the field of software testing. It aims to provide testing professionals with a systematic body of knowledge, helping them effectively use generative AI technologies to improve testing efficiency and quality.

The syllabus authors are: Abbas Ahmad, Gualtiero Bazzana, Alessandro Collino, Olivier Denoo, and Bruno Legeard

The following content is organized based on the syllabus and can be used as a reference.

Certification Background and Objectives

Core Value Positioning

The CT-GenAI certification is intended for all professionals involved in software testing, including:

  • Test engineers, test analysts, test automation engineers
  • Test managers, user acceptance testers, software developers
  • Project managers, quality managers, software development managers
  • Business analysts, IT directors, and management consultants

Five Key Business Outcomes

Professionals who obtain this certification will have the following core capabilities:

  1. Understand the basic concepts, capabilities, and limitations of generative AI
  2. Master large language model prompt engineering skills for software testing
  3. Identify and mitigate the risks of generative AI in software testing
  4. Understand the applications of generative AI solutions in software testing
  5. Effectively participate in the formulation and implementation of generative AI testing strategies within the organization

Certification Content System

Chapter 1: Fundamentals of Generative AI in Software Testing

Core Concepts of Generative AI

  • AI technology lineage: The differences and application scenarios of symbolic AI, classical machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI
  • Large Language Model (LLM) fundamentals:
    • Tokenization and Embedding technologies
    • The concept of Context Window and its impact
    • Non-deterministic behavior characteristics
  • LLM classification system:
    • Foundation LLMs
    • Instruction-Tuned LLMs
    • Reasoning LLMs
  • Multimodal LLMs and Vision-Language Models: The ability to process multimodal data such as text, images, and audio

Core Capabilities of Generative AI in Testing

  • Requirements analysis and improvement: Identify ambiguity, inconsistency, and missing information in requirements
  • Test case generation: Create test cases based on system requirements or user stories
  • Test oracle generation: Automatically generate expected results
  • Test data generation: Create datasets, boundary values, and test data combinations
  • Test automation support: Generate test scripts from test case descriptions
  • Test result analysis: Create summaries and classify anomalies by severity and priority
  • Test artifact creation: Generate test plans, test reports, and defect reports

Comparison of Interaction Modes

  • AI chatbots: Provide a natural-language interaction interface, suitable for quick feedback and concept clarification
  • LLM-driven testing applications: Enable automated testing tasks through API integration, supporting customization and scalability

Chapter 2: Prompt Engineering for Effective Software Testing

Effective Prompt Generation

  • Six elements of prompt structure:
    1. Role: Define the perspective the AI should adopt (e.g., tester, test manager)
    2. Context: Provide the test object and background information
    3. Instruction: Specify the task to be performed
    4. Input Data: Provide specific test materials
    5. Constraints: Set limits and rules
    6. Output Format: Specify the desired response format

Core Prompting Techniques

  • Zero-shot Prompting: Request a task directly without examples
  • Few-shot Prompting: Provide a small number of examples to guide the AI
  • Prompt Chaining: Break a complex task down into multiple sequential prompts
  • Meta Prompting: Guide the AI on how to think about the task itself

Test Task Applications

  • Test analysis: Use multimodal prompts to generate acceptance criteria for GUI wireframes
  • Test design and implementation:
    • Generate functional test cases from user stories
    • Use few-shot prompting to generate Gherkin-style test conditions
    • Determine test case priorities through prompt chaining
  • Automated regression testing:
    • Create and manage keyword-driven test scripts
    • Analyze test reports with structured prompts
  • Test monitoring and control: Generate monitoring metrics based on test data

Chapter 3: Managing the Risks of Generative AI in Software Testing

Key Risk Types

  1. Hallucinations and reasoning errors:
    • Identify factual errors and logical flaws in LLM output
    • Mitigation techniques: fact-checking, multi-model verification, human review
  2. Data privacy and security risks:
    • Privacy vulnerabilities in test data and tools
    • Mitigation strategies: data masking, local deployment, access control
  3. Energy consumption and environmental impact:
    • Assess the energy consumption and carbon emissions of GenAI usage
    • Optimize model usage efficiency and reduce resource waste

Compliance Framework

  • AI regulations and standards: EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 38507, etc.
  • Best practice frameworks: Responsible AI usage guidelines, ethical testing principles

Chapter 4: LLM-Driven Testing Infrastructure

Architectural Approaches

  • Key architectural components:
    • Model service layer
    • Prompt engineering layer
    • Result evaluation layer
    • Integration interface layer
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Combine external knowledge bases to improve response accuracy
  • LLM-driven testing agents: Intelligent agents that automate the testing process

Model Optimization and Operations

  • Fine-Tuning: Optimize LLMs for specific testing tasks
  • LLMOps (Large Language Model Operations):
    • Model deployment and version management
    • Performance monitoring and optimization
    • Cost control strategies

Chapter 5: Deployment and Integration of Generative AI in Testing Organizations

Adoption Roadmap

  • Shadow AI risks: Security risks brought by the use of unapproved AI tools
  • Key strategic elements:
    • Define clear business goals and value propositions
    • Select suitable LLMs/SLMs (Small Language Models)
    • Phased implementation plan
  • Adoption stages:
    1. Pilot and proof of concept
    2. Technical capability building
    3. Process integration
    4. Scale-up and promotion

Change Management

  • Core skills and knowledge:
    • Prompt engineering skills
    • AI ethics and risk awareness
    • Test automation and AI integration skills
  • Team capability building:
    • Develop training plans
    • Build communities of practice
    • Bring in external experts
  • Evolution of testing processes:
    • Integration of traditional testing processes with AI-enhanced processes
    • Define new roles and responsibilities
    • Continuous improvement mechanisms

Certification System and Exam Requirements

Cognitive Level Classification

  • K1 (Remember): Identify and recall terms and concepts
  • K2 (Understand): Explain and compare concepts and relationships
  • K3 (Apply): Apply knowledge and skills in specific situations

Practical Objective Levels

  • H0: Demonstration observation (not performed by the learner)
  • H1: Guided practice (the learner follows instructions)
  • H2: Practice with prompts (completed independently by the learner)

Exam Requirements

  • Prerequisite: Hold an ISTQB® Foundation Level certificate
  • Exam content: Based on all chapters of this syllabus (except the introduction and appendices)
  • Exam format: Multiple-choice questions requiring the integrated application of knowledge from multiple chapters

Certification Value and Applicable Scenarios

Career Development Path

The CT-GenAI certification is an important part of the ISTQB® Expert Level certification system, and holders can continue to advance:

  • Advanced Level certifications: Test Analyst, Technical Test Analyst, Test Manager, Test Engineer
  • Expert Level certifications: Test Management, Test Process Improvement

Industry Application Value

  1. Efficiency improvement: Reduce repetitive testing work through AI automation
  2. Quality enhancement: Use AI analytical capabilities to find deeper defects
  3. Cost optimization: Allocate testing resources reasonably and reduce overall testing costs
  4. Innovation drive: Explore new application scenarios of AI in the testing field
  5. Risk management: Systematically identify and mitigate risks related to AI testing

Conclusion

As generative AI technology continues to evolve, testing professionals need to continuously update their knowledge systems. While enjoying the efficiency gains brought by AI, they must maintain a deep understanding of the essence of testing — ensuring the quality and reliability of software products.

Learning about the CT-GenAI certification can serve as a reference for a systematic body of knowledge and a practical guide.

For certification details, you can refer to the official ISTQB website in China: CSTQB

https://www.cstqb.cn/
